# Robert Jacomb-Hood

**Robert Jacomb-Hood** MICE (25 January 1822 – 10 May 1900) was a British civil engineer and railway executive. He served as the Resident Engineer and later a director of the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway (LB&SCR). His career spanned the mid-19th century expansion of the British railway network, during which he oversaw the construction of major infrastructure including the LB&SCR's terminus at London Victoria station and the expansion of London Bridge station.

Jacomb-Hood was a recognized contributor to the professional development of railway engineering. He was awarded the Telford Medal by the Institution of Civil Engineers in 1858 for his work on the design and logistics of railway stations, advocating for functionality and "judicious arrangement" over architectural ornamentation.

## Early life and education

Robert Jacomb-Hood was born on 25 January 1822 at Riseley in Bedfordshire . He was the eldest son of Robert Jacomb, a yeoman farmer who later assumed the surname Hood. In 1833, his father inherited the Bardon Park estate in Leicestershire from a cousin, William Hood, and subsequently adopted the name Jacomb-Hood .

Jacomb-Hood received his early education at Christ's Hospital. Following his father's wish for him to pursue a legal career, he attended Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1840 and 1841. However, influenced by interactions with peers engaged in railway construction in the Midlands, he developed an interest in engineering. He eventually persuaded his father to allow him to leave the university to pursue this profession .

In 1841, he became an articled pupil of George Watson Buck, the Chief Engineer of the Manchester and Birmingham Railway. During his apprenticeship, he worked as an assistant on the Holmes Chapel section of the line under William Baker, and on the Crewe section under William Henry Barlow .

## Career

### Early engineering work
Following the opening of the Manchester and Birmingham line to Crewe in 1843, Jacomb-Hood was retained as a Chief Assistant by George Watson Buck, who had moved into private practice in Manchester. During this period, Jacomb-Hood worked on the rebuilding of the New Bailey Bridge in Salford. He later returned to the Manchester and Birmingham Railway as an assistant to William Baker for the construction of the Macclesfield branch. Between 1844 and 1846, he served as the Resident Engineer on the Manchester, South Junction and Altrincham Railway .

### London, Brighton and South Coast Railway (1846–1860)
In 1846, following the amalgamation that formed the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway (LB&SCR), Jacomb-Hood was appointed Resident Engineer for the entire system. He held this position for fourteen years, a period characterized by the rapid development of the company's infrastructure .

During his tenure, he oversaw the completion of the new London Bridge station and the Bricklayers Arms goods station. He was responsible for laying out and completing numerous branch lines, including those to Newhaven, Eastbourne, Hailsham, Epsom, Croydon, Wandsworth, Littlehampton, and Steyning . Between 1850 and 1860, he also managed the construction of the Crystal Palace branch, the East Grinstead branch, and lines serving Lewes, Uckfield, Shoreham, and Henfield .

One of his most significant projects was the design and construction of the LB&SCR's portion of London Victoria station, which opened on 1 October 1860 . The station was a joint venture with the London, Chatham and Dover Railway (LCDR), but the two companies built separate stations side-by-side. Jacomb-Hood designed the roof of the Brighton side, which was noted for its cost-effectiveness; it was constructed for approximately £17 per square (100 sq ft), roughly two-thirds the cost of the adjacent roof designed by John Fowler for the LCDR .

### Private practice and directorships
Due to the increasing pressure of parliamentary work associated with railway expansion, Jacomb-Hood resigned as Resident Engineer in September 1860. He retained a role consulting on parliamentary and new works while establishing a private practice in Westminster .

In 1865, he entered into a partnership with his cousin and former pupil, William Jacomb. Together, they developed schemes for various railways, including the Surrey and Sussex, West Kent, and lines connecting Norwood to the Crystal Palace High Level station. The partnership was dissolved in 1870 when William Jacomb was appointed Chief Engineer of the London and South Western Railway .

Jacomb-Hood held several directorships during his later career. He became a director of the Crystal Palace Company in 1869, serving until 1879, during which time he was involved in the construction of the Crystal Palace Aquarium. In 1870, he joined the board of the Anglo-Maltese Hydraulic Dock Company, occasionally travelling to Malta to inspect the company's affairs .

He renewed his close association with the LB&SCR in March 1883, when he was invited to join the company's board of directors following the retirement of Sir Arthur Otway. He remained a director until his death, devoting his final years to the administration of the railway .

## Professional contributions and awards

Jacomb-Hood was an active member of the Institution of Civil Engineers (ICE), having been elected a member in March 1847 . He contributed technical papers that reflected his practical experience with railway infrastructure.

### Vertical Lift Bridge (1850)
In 1850, he presented a paper titled *Description of a Vertical Lift Bridge erected over the Grand Surrey Canal*. This work detailed the engineering of a lifting bridge on the Thames Junction Branch of the LB&SCR. The bridge utilized a timber platform balanced by counterweights and operated by hand-gearing, allowing it to be raised to provide clearance for barges on the canal . For this paper, the Institution awarded him a Council Premium of Books .

### Railway Station Design (1858)
In 1858, Jacomb-Hood presented a paper titled *The Arrangement and Construction of Railway Stations*. In this text, he argued that the design of stations should be the domain of engineers rather than architects. He introduced the concept of "judicious arrangement," positing that the functionality and logistical efficiency of a station were superior to architectural grandeur . He was awarded the Telford Medal, the ICE's highest prize, for this contribution .

## Personal life and death

Jacomb-Hood married Jane Stothard Littlewood in the early 1850s. She was the daughter of George Littlewood, a printer . The couple had several children. Their son, George Percy Jacomb-Hood (1857–1929), became a painter and illustrator . Another son, John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood (1859–1914), followed his father into the engineering profession, eventually becoming the Chief Engineer of the London and South Western Railway .

Robert Jacomb-Hood died suddenly on 10 May 1900 at his residence in Tunbridge Wells, at the age of 78. He had been transacting business for the Brighton Company on the day of his death .

This material is largely derived from Len Noble's book (published 1995) "Bardon Hill  - a source book being a collection of papers, anecdotes and published work concerning the anceint enclosure of Bardon Park with additional comment".       ISBN 0 9525978 0 2

Following the invasion and conquest of England in 1066 by William of Normandy, the manor of Whitwick was one of many in Leicestershire granted to Hugh de Grandmesnil (1032 - 1098), who had been one of William of Normandy's trusted supporters at the Battle of Hastings.

In 1204, in the reign of King John, the castle at Whitwick was put in the hands of a keeper named William de Senevill.

The manor passed from Hugh de Grandmesnil through the earls of Leicester to Roger de Quincey, earl of Winton (or Winchester).   (The earls of Leicester and Winton/Winchester were descendants of Hugh de Grandmesnil).  On Roger de Quincey's death in 1264, the manor passed through his daughter Elizabeth to her Scottish husband Alexander Comyn, earl of Buchan.   (Incidentally, Elizabeth's sister Helen de Quincey married Alan de la Zouch).

Alexander made over the manor of Whitwick to his eldest son John Comyn and his wife in 1282.

John Comyn was a rebel.   The Crown disapproved of his support of John Balliol's claim to the Scottish crown.

John Comyn's wife Isabel McDuff was daughter of the McDuff earl of Fife.   The McDuff earls of Fife were regarded as having the ancient right to crown the Scottish kings.

After an abortive raid on Carlisle in 1299, John Comyn was ordered to dwell south of the Trent until the end of the war with France.  Some of his lordships were taken from him and John de Barr was given custody of the manor of Whitwick.

It is recorded that in 1300 John de Barr was given licence to sell wood from the park at Bardon.

The manor of Whitwick was restored to John Comyn in 1304.

John Comyn's kinsman, the Red Comyn, was himself one of a number of rival contenders for the throne of Scotland.

On 10th February 1306, the Red Comyn was murdered by Robert the Bruce, another rival contender.   This brutal murder took place in the Greyfriars monastery church at Dumfries, in front of the Holy Table.

Events then moved very quickly, and at Scone in March 1306 Robert Bruce was crowned king of Scotland.    In fact, he was crowned twice, once on 25th March, and with a second coronation on 29th March, as explained below.

In 1306, Isabel's father (Duncan III) was dead (murdered, circa 1289), and her brother, the then current McDuff earl of Fife (Duncan IV) was still a minor.   Further, Duncan IV he was not available to take part in a coronation ceremony in that he was captive in English hands.

There was a form of coronation at Scone on 25th March 1203, with much formaility and ceremony, but potentially its validity may have been open to challenge in that the young McDuff earl of Fife was not and could not be present, nor was he represented.

As explained, John Comyn's wife Isabel McDuff was the daughter of the murdered McDuff earl of Fife (Duncan III), and sister to the current imprisoned young earl (Duncan IV).

A second coronation ceremony was held on 29 March 1306 when Isabel McDuff turned up at Scone.  Opposing her husband whose cousin the Bruce had so recently murdered, and claiming to act on behalf of her captive brother Duncan IV, the current McDuff earl of Fife, and her murdered father Duncan III, Isabel placed the Scottich Crown on the head of Robert the Bruce !!!

Two years later, Robert the Bruce soundly defeated John Comyn who was forced to retire to England where he died in 1308, without issue.   Isabel was imprisoned at Berwick on Tweed on the orders of King Edward II.  She remained there until 1313.   It is recorded that Isabel was kept in a cage suspended from the walls of Berwick Castle.

John Comyn's heirs were Margaret Comyn and Alice Comyn, the daughters of John's brother Alexander Comyn, earl of Buchan.    In 1301, Alice Comyn had married Henry, Lord Beaumont.  Alice should have taken her share of her inheritance from John Comyn.   However, John's brother William had, with his brother's consent, taken possession of some parts of the manors concerned, including Bardon Park.   This transfer could only happen if the King gave consent, which was eventually given, and so the manors concerned were then officially delivered to the Beaumonts.

In 1313, Edmund de Hastings was ordered to deliver John Comyn's widow Isabel from Berwick on Tweed to the keeping of Henry Beaumont who, as we have seen, was married to a Comyn (Alice Comyn) and was eventually lord of the manor of Whitwick.

The name Hastings will be repeated in the later history of Bardon Park.

In 1326, the lords of the manors of Loughborough, Hugglescote, Shepshed and Beaumanor were executed for treason, and the Beaumonts succeeded to the titles.   The Beaumonts then deserted Whitwick and Bardon, leaving them to rot.

Henry Beaumont had fought alongside the king at Boroughbridge (battle of Boroughbridge, 16th March 1322), but in 1326 he too betrayed the king.   As a result, the king (King Edward II) was detained at Berkley Castle (Gloucestershire) and murdered (1327).

After Alice and Margaret Comyn inherited, the manorial benefits had been divided.  Over the years they were to be divided again and again.  It is not at all clear to whose benefit the park at Bardon fell.

Henry Beaumont died in 1339.   He was succeeded by his 22 year old son John who had married Eleanor, daughter of the earl of Lancaster.  John died in 1342, leaving a two year old son Henry as heir.

The succession of Henry at the age of two in 1342 was the first of four generations of Beaumont minors to succeed to the lordships.   Henry Beaumont died in 1369 at the age of 29, leaving as heir his eight year old son, John, who died in 1396 at the age of 35, leaving his son 16 year old Henry, as lord of the manor.  In his turn Henry died in 1413 at the age of 33 leaving yet another minor, John aged three to succeed.

The last Henry Beaumont's widow, Elizabeth, held the lordships until her death in 1427 when the inquisition noted that Whitwick castle was "old and ruinous, in which are no buildings and worth nothing yearly".   The manor was then in a poor state and the note records "there are 12 messuages there, of which 12 are in the lord's hands for want of tenants".  Bardon Park is not mentioned.

John Beaumont was 18 on his mother's death.   He was to prove a family exception.   He married Elizabeth, sole heir of Sir William Phelip, lord Bardolf.

On 12 February 1439, John Beaumont was the first viscount ever to be created.   In 1441, he was made a knight of the Garter.   In the same year, hs wife Elizabeth died leaving a son named William who, having inherited his maternal grandmother's estates, was during his father's lifetime known as "lord Bardolf".   John Beaumont then married Katerine, daughter of Ralph, duke of Westmoreland who, because of a previous marriage to John de Mowbray, duke of Norfolk, retained the title "duchess" for the rest of her life.   (Katerine had also been married to Sir Thomas Strangeways).  John Beaumont, her third husband, was killed at the battle of Northampton on 10 july 1461.  He was 41 years old.

William (lord Bardolf), who became second viscount Beaumont, was (like his father) on the Lancastrian side in the wars of the roses.   He was taken prisoner at the battle of Towton in 1461.  In the same year by Act of Parliament he forfeited all of his estates and in 1462 these were put in the hands of the king's servitor Richard Hastings.    This was only a temporary arrangement for, in 1485, Henry VII restored the possessions and lordships to the Beaumonts.

In 1486, William made over the manors of Whitwick and Markfield to "Katherine Hastyngs, widow, lady hastyngs, and Edward hastyngs, knight, lord Hastyngs during the life of the said Katherine".    It is not clear why William should have made this transfer.   One possible reason would be if Katherine Beaumont had been married to Edward Hastyngs, as her fourth husband.   Was this Katherine, William Beaumont's step-mother ?    There is another possible reason.  In 1487, William Beaumont had been declared mad.  He was given into the custody of John de Vere, earl of Oxford.

In 1507, William Beaumont died at the age of 69 at the earl of Oxford's house at Wivenhoe.   One historian says the estates and lordships then reverted to the Crown as William Beaumont had died without issue.    Another historian says that John de Vere succeeded to the lordships through his wife Elizabeth who was the daughter of William Beaumont.

At this time there were four dwellings in the Park.

The manor of Whitwick again reverted to the Crown.   This time due to the treasonable acts of Francis, Lord Lovel.

In 1512, the then king, Henry VIII, exchanged the manor of Whitwick for lands in Kent with Thomas Grey, second marquis of Dorset.  This Thomas's father (also Thomas) had been created marquis of Dorset in 1475, after his widowed mother (the second marquis's grandmother) married the king and became Queen Elizabeth Woodville.

The second marquis was succeeded by his son Henry, who had been created duke of Suffolk; thus Henry was first duke of Suffolk and third marquis of Dorset.  Henry was the father of Lady Jane Grey.

After being convicted of treason, Suffolk lost the family's right to the manor.  He was beheaded on 23 February 1554.

On the death of the dowager duchess of Suffolk in 1559, the manor reverted to the Crown and in 1604 William Kyngeston became bailiff of the manor of Whitwick.

In 1612, King James I (James VI of Scotland) sold the manor for £ 4000 to Sir Henry Hastings and Henry Cutler and their heirs, in trust for Henry, earl of Huntingdon.

This 1612 transfer is intriguing.   King Robert the Bruce was a grandson of an earlier earl of Huntingdon !!!

The manor of Whitwick was then held by the Hastings family until the end of the 19th century.

This possession of the manor of Whitwick meant that Bardon Park was at the disposal of Hastings and Cutler until they sold the Park to the Hood family, who had been for some years resident there as tenants.

The earliest written record of the Hood family at Bardon Park is that of the marriage of Thomas Hood in 1574 to Elizabeth.

The Hoods remained at Bardon Park until the death of old William Hood at nearly ninety years of age on 16 May 1833.

Under the terms of William's Will, the Bardon Park estate passed to his cousin Robert Jacomb.   The link between the Hoods and the Jacombs derives from William Hood's father John Hood and Robert Jacomb's grandfather William Jacomb, and is explained below:

*   *   John Hood and William Jacomb had been London solicitors in practice together.
        
    *   They (John Hood and William Jacomb) had married two sisters Cecelia Snell and Mary Snell (grand-daughters of Sir Edmund Harrison).   Robert Jacomb was the grandson of William Jacomb and Mary Snell, and thus William Hood and Robert Jacomb were cousins (first-cousins-once-removed), through William Hood's mother Cecelia Snell and Robert Jacomb's paternal grandmother Mary Snell.
        
    *   There is also a family link on the paternal (Hood) side, in that Sarah Danvers had been the first wife to Robert Jacomb's father, the Reverend Robert Jacomb.   William Hood and Sarah Danvers were cousins (first-cousins-once-removed), through William Hood's paternal aunt Elizabeth Hood (Mrs Danvers), grandmother to Sarah Danvers.    Incidentally, Elizabeth was killed by the fall of the chimney at her house in Bath, occasioned by the high wind on 14th March 1757 known as 'Byng's Wind'.
        

Upon inheriting the Bardon Park estate from William Hood, Robert Jacomb and his wife Susan took the hyphenated name Jacomb-Hood.      They moved to Bardon Park in 1834.   In 1836, they set about building a grand new hall on the hillside.   They moved into the new hall in 1837, and the dilapidated ancient hall on the moated island in the shallow valley to the south of the hill was demolished around 1840.

*   *   A son and grandson of Robert and Susan became noted civil and railway engineers.  A cousin William Jacomb (1831-1887) had been articled in 1851 to Isambard Kingdom Brunel (1806-1859).   Robert and Susan's eldest son (also Robert), Robert Jacomb-Hood Jnr (1822-1900), took articles with William Jacomb.   Their grandson John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood (1859-1914) then followed his father into the civil and railway engineering profession.  Between the three of them (William Jacomb, Robert Jacomb-Hood and John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood) they were responsible for the construction of several Thames bridges and Waterloo Station.
        
    *   The noted portrait and genre painter and illustrator and etcher George Percy Jacomb-Hood (1857-1929) was John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood's elder brother.
        
    *   In 1885, Robert and Susan's daughter Miss Eliza Jacomb-Hood (1826-1889) donated a 37 foot lifeboat to the RNLI station at Newbiggin-by-Sea in Northumberland in  memory of her parents.   The Robert and Susan lifeboat was the fourth boat at the Newbiggin station where it served until 1906.   During that time, it saved 79 lives.  A model, originally presented to Miss Eliza, may be seen at the RNLI museum at Newbiggin.
        

In 1859, Robert and Susan tried to sell the Bardon Park estate.    The estate was eventually sold, apparently in 1864, to the Herrick family.

From about the 1870s onwards, the Herrick family leased and/or sold certain quarrying rights to Messrs Ellis & Everard.

Mr Breedon Everard moved to Hill Top House (later called Bardon Hill House) in about 1856.   From about 1872 until about 1939, members of the Everard family occupied Bardon Hall as tenants.

The Curzon-Herrick family sold the Bardon estate by auction on 28th August 1947, and the estate was broken-up.

The Tom family, a Cornish family of quarrymnasters, bought into the Ellis & Everard quarrying company, and eventually gained control of the company.   Most of Bardon Park was later bought by the Tom family and their company Bardon Hill Quarries Limited.   This company is now re-named Aggregate Industries, and is part of a world-wide group of companies, the Holcim group.

John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood (1859-1914), chief engineer of the [London and South Western Railway](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/London_and_South_Western_Railway "London and South Western Railway")

1859 Born in Lewisham, son of [Robert Jacomb-Hood](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Robert_Jacomb-Hood "Robert Jacomb-Hood"), civil engineer[\[1\]](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/John_Wykeham_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-1)

* * *

**1914 Obituary [\[2\]](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/John_Wykeham_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-2)**

JOHN WYKEHAM JACOMB-HOOD was born in 1859 and was educated at Tonbridge School and at the Crystal Palace School of Engineering.

He became a pupil to the then chief engineer to the London & South-Western Railway Company in 1875.

From 1878 to 1887 he served in the capacity of assistant engineer to the Company, carrying out the construction of various new works.

For the next eight years he was District Engineer in charge of the way and works in the London district, afterwards being transferred in 1895 to the Western district.

In 1901 he became Chief Resident Engineer, a position that he held until his death, which took place suddenly at a meet of the Dulverton Hounds on the 6th March, 1914. He was responsible for the carrying out and maintenance of much of the electrical work of the Company, and took great interest in the question of electrification. In recent years his most important work was in connection with the enlargement and reconstruction of [Waterloo Station](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/index.php?title=Water;oo_Railway_Station&action=edit&redlink=1 "Water;oo Railway Station (page does not exist)").

He was elected a Member of the Institution in 1904.

**Robert Jacomb-Hood**[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-3) [MICE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Institution_of_Civil_Engineers "Member of the Institution of Civil Engineers") (25 January 1822 – 10 May 1900) was a British civil engineer who rose to prominence as the first Resident Engineer of the [London, Brighton and South Coast Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London,_Brighton_and_South_Coast_Railway "London, Brighton and South Coast Railway") (LB&SCR), a position he held from the company's amalgamation in 1846 until 1860. During this time, he was responsible for projects including [London Victoria station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station "London Victoria station"), [London Bridge station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge_station "London Bridge station"), and [Crystal Palace railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Palace_railway_station "Crystal Palace railway station"), as well as a large number of branch lines across the south of England.

Born to a working-class family in Bedfordshire, Jacomb-Hood's father inherited an estate from his cousin in 1833, drastically improving the financial situation of the family. Jacomb-Hood was removed from [Christ's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ%27s_Hospital "Christ's Hospital") in favour of private tuition before attending the [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge") to study Law. However, he quickly dropped out to become a railway engineer instead, rising through their ranks quickly under the guidance of [George W. Buck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Buck "George W. Buck"). He was selected as the fist Resident Engineer of the LB&SCR in 1846, only five years after he entered the industry. The finances of the company were tumultuous, with some years seeing strong gains and others so poor that Jacomb-Hood narrowly escaped being fired. However, his career personal finances grew steadily and he was elected a Member of the [Institution of Civil Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institution_of_Civil_Engineers "Institution of Civil Engineers") in 1847.

After transitioning to practising privately in 1860, he began partnering with a variety of engineers and architects including [Charles Driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Driver "Charles Driver"), [George Parker Bidder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Parker_Bidder_/(engineer/) "George Parker Bidder (engineer)"), and his cousin Wililam Jacomb. He also expanded his work outside of railway engineering, working on projects such as the [National Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery "National Gallery") and the Portcreek Viaduct. However, the death of his first wife and the end of his joint practice with Jacomb motivated him to enter semi-retirement; as part of this, he switched his focus from designing and constructing projects in the UK to joining companies' [boards of directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors") and taking up international opportunities. This included significant contributions to the [Crystal Palace Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") between 1869 and 1880, as well as the [Alabama Great Southern Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_Great_Southern_Railroad "Alabama Great Southern Railroad") which he helped to create and sat as a member of the board between 1877 and 1886.

In 1883 he returned to the LB&SCR as a member of the board; by this time, he was barely working and instead spending most of his time travelling the world. He slowly left the companies he had been a board member of; his last known attendance at a civil engineering project was in 1894, but he continued assisting the LB&SCR until his death in 1900 aged 78. Over his extensive six-decade career, he saw success not only as the designer and engineer of railway projects, but as the director and important figure of various companies across four continents. He also saw academic success, being awarded two of the Institution of Civil Engineers' accolades in 1850 and 1858 respectfully, the latter of which was for a paper that was considered pioneering in station design and [railway engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_engineering "Railway engineering").

[![Image 3: A medieval church surrounded by a cemetery. There are trees in the right foreground and left background, and a blue sky](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/St_Mary_and_All_Saints_Church%2C_Stambridge_Road%2C_Great_Stambridge_%28NHLE_Code_1168425%29_%28May_2024%29_%282%29.jpg/250px-St_Mary_and_All_Saints_Church%2C_Stambridge_Road%2C_Great_Stambridge_%28NHLE_Code_1168425%29_%28May_2024%29_%282%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Mary_and_All_Saints_Church,_Stambridge_Road,_Great_Stambridge_/(NHLE_Code_1168425/)_/(May_2024/)_/(2/).jpg)

St Mary and All Saints Church in [Great Stambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stambridge "Great Stambridge"), where Jacomb-Hood's parents married.

Jacomb-Hood was born on 25 January 1822 at The Lodge Farm in [Riseley, Bedfordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riseley,_Bedfordshire "Riseley, Bedfordshire").[\[‡ 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-4) He was also [baptised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptised "Baptised") in Riseley,[\[‡ 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-5) with unpublished material from the Christ's Hospital school archives suggesting this was on 21 February 1822.[\[‡ 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-christs-hospital-school-london-archives-6) He was the first of his parents' nine children;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58  according to their marriage certificate, they had married on 29 March 1819 at St Mary And All Saints Church in [Great Stambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stambridge "Great Stambridge"), Essex.[\[‡ 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-8)

Jacomb-Hood's mother was Susan Jacomb-Hood ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Kemp), the daughter of John Kemp of Broomhills in [Rochford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochford "Rochford"), Essex.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-walford-9)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-10) His mother's brother—George Tawke Kemp—owned the Beechhill estate, also situated in Rochford, and his son [George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Kemp,_1st_Baron_Rochdale "George Kemp, 1st Baron Rochdale") was given the title [Baron Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_Rochdale "Baron Rochdale") on 14 February 1913.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-11)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-12)

Jacomb-Hood's father was Robert Jacomb, who began his career as a [yeoman farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeoman "Yeoman").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-sellingantiques-13) As of 1822, he was a [tenant farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenant_farmer "Tenant farmer") on land belonging to [John Russell, 6th Duke of Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Russell,_6th_Duke_of_Bedford "John Russell, 6th Duke of Bedford").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 51  On the 1833 death of his cousin, the [barrister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrister "Barrister") William Hood,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-:0-14) Jacomb inherited Hood's estate at [Bardon Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bardon_Hall "Bardon Hall") in Bardon, [Leicestershire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicestershire "Leicestershire");[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-:0-14)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-bulletin-of-the-loughborough-and-district-archaeological-society-1981-15) this was because Hood was the last male member of his family. Jacomb had no link to the estate and his interest in its ownership was only because of the financial benefit.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-bulletin-of-the-loughborough-and-district-archaeological-society-1981-15) However, this inheritance was on the condition that Jacomb took the surname of Hood, becoming Robert Jacomb-Hood,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-:0-14) because the estate had been in the Hood family since the 1620s.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-sellingantiques-13) Jacomb-Hood modified the estate by building a New Hall in 1835 and demolishing the Old Hall building around 1840,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-bulletin-of-the-loughborough-and-district-archaeological-society-1981-15) which he had described in his memoirs as "too dilapidated for residence, and the situation was low, damp and unhealthy".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-noble-1995-16) He was accepted to the [Worshipful Company of Fan Makers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worshipful_Company_of_Fan_Makers "Worshipful Company of Fan Makers")—one of the 113 [livery companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livery_company "Livery company") of the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London")[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-17)—on 9 January 1832.[\[‡ 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-christs-hospital-school-london-archives-6)

Jacomb-Hood's first education was by a private tutor in [Dereham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dereham "Dereham"), Norfolk when he was aged seven.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 51  He then entered [Christ's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ%27s_Hospital "Christ's Hospital"), a [public school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_school_/(United_Kingdom/) "Public school (United Kingdom)")[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-19) in [West Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Sussex "West Sussex").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) [\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 51  Unpublished archive material stored by the school suggests that Jacomb-Hood's father applied for his place in December 1831, by which time he had three siblings. His father's income at the time of the application was reported to "not exceed £100 per annum",[\[‡ 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-christs-hospital-school-london-archives-6) which equates to a salary of below £11,470 in 2023.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21) Jacomb-Hood was admitted to the school on 13 January 1832, aged nine. His family did not pay for his education or any associated fees; instead, he was sponsored by George Green, the governor for donations at the school. Starting at the preparatory school in [Hertford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertford "Hertford"), Hertfordshire,[\[‡ 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-christs-hospital-school-london-archives-6) Jacomb-Hood then moved to the main school in [Newgate Street, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgate_Street,_London "Newgate Street, London") in 1834.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 51 [\[‡ 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-christs-hospital-school-london-archives-6)

According to the school archives, of the three departments at the school, Jacomb-Hood belonged to the Writing School, which was for children wanting to pursue financial or commercial work. There, he was considered best out of 258 students for [penmanship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penmanship "Penmanship") on 25 November 1834,[\[‡ 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-christs-hospital-school-london-archives-6) for which he was awarded a golden pen, the school's equivalent of first prize.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 51  As a result of his father's inheritance of Bardon Hall, he was removed from the school on 6 November 1835;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 51 [\[‡ 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-christs-hospital-school-london-archives-6) he was signed out by a 'J A Kemp', who would have been on his mother's side of the family. None of his siblings attended the school.[\[‡ 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-christs-hospital-school-london-archives-6)

After leaving Christ's Hospital, Jacomb-Hood was educated by [Reverend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Reverend "The Reverend") H. Richardson, who was the [rector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rector_/(ecclesiastical/) "Rector (ecclesiastical)") of [Leire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leire "Leire"), Leicestershire. However, Jacomb-Hood's father was not happy with the quality of his tuition and moved him to Wood & Throwgood School in [Totteridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totteridge "Totteridge"), Hertfordshire in 1836. By this time, the family were living in Bardon Park and his father was undertaking renovation works. Between 1839 and 1840, Jacomb-Hood was educated in [Hathern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hathern "Hathern"), Leicestershire, as a precursor to him studying at the [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"). At the same time, the family moved to [Cheltenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheltenham "Cheltenham"), Gloucestershire; in both locations, Jacomb-Hood witnessed railway construction; those were the [Birmingham and Gloucester Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_and_Gloucester_Railway "Birmingham and Gloucester Railway") in Cheltenham and the [Midland Counties Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midland_Counties_Railway "Midland Counties Railway") in Hathern. In his diaries, he recalls visiting the sites with his friends, and that they served as an inspiration for his choice of career.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 51–2

Jacomb-Hood's father wanted him to pursue a career as a [barrister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrister "Barrister"), and had discouraged his son's interest in engineering; at first, Jacomb-Hood respected his father's wishes, choosing to study [law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_degree "Law degree").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 51–2  He was admitted to [Trinity College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College,_Cambridge "Trinity College, Cambridge") on 25 May 1840 and he began his degree the same year.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-venn-1947-22) He is listed in _[Alumni Cantabrigienses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alumni_Cantabrigienses "Alumni Cantabrigienses")_ as a pensioner (full fee-paying student) and described to be of "of Bardon Park, Leics".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-venn-1947-22) However, after what Alan A. Jackson describes as a "couple of unsuccessful terms", Jacomb-Hood dropped out of the University in April 1841,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52  instead choosing to become a railway engineer.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52

### 1841–1846: Early career

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Jacomb-Hood&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1841–1846: Early career")\]

After dropping out of University, Jacomb-Hood scheduled an interview with civil engineer [Charles Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Fox_/(engineer,_born_1810/) "Charles Fox (engineer, born 1810)") to join his company Fox & Henderson. However, his former classmate from his education in Hathern, Albert Pell, had been employed at the company; Pell warned Jacomb-Hood to avoid working as an engineer for Fox. He then tried to get a job from [John Birkinshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Birkinshaw "John Birkinshaw"), who worked under [Robert Stephenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stephenson "Robert Stephenson") on the [Birmingham and Derby Junction Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_and_Derby_Junction_Railway "Birmingham and Derby Junction Railway"); however, Birkinshaw was ill and thus unable to meet Jacomb-Hood, something which the latter described in his diaries as "fortunate".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52  Finally, he managed successfully to become the student of the railway engineer [George W. Buck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Buck "George W. Buck"), who at the time was the Chief Engineer of the [Manchester and Birmingham Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_and_Birmingham_Railway "Manchester and Birmingham Railway") (M&BR) alongside Robert Stephenson.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52

Upon becoming a student of Buck, he was tasked to work under [draftsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draftsman "Draftsman") Charles Heard Wild to make the technical drawings for the railway for a period of nine months. In his diaries, Jacomb-Hood speaks of both Wild and Buck very highly, describing them as "'one of the cleverest draftsmen" and "a most excellent master" respectively.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52  He was then sent by Buck to [Sandbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandbach "Sandbach") to work as the assistant to William Baker,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52  who was responsible for a stretch of what would become the [Crewe–Manchester line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crewe%E2%80%93Manchester_line "Crewe–Manchester line") near [Holmes Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmes_Chapel_railway_station "Holmes Chapel railway station").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) By the time the line reached [Crewe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crewe_railway_station "Crewe railway station") in 1843, Buck had stopped working for the M&BR and was instead practicing privately in Manchester; he then employed Jacomb-Hood as his Chief Assistant.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52

[![Image 4: A photograph of a bridge over a road with cars and people on the road. The bridge is built with repeating patterns of red, black, and white.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Salford_Central_Railway_Bridge_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1414987.jpg/250px-Salford_Central_Railway_Bridge_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1414987.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Salford_Central_Railway_Bridge_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1414987.jpg)

The [Salford Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salford_Central_railway_station "Salford Central railway station") railway bridges, which Jacomb-Hood engineered.

During his time as Chief Assistant to Buck, Jacomb-Hood was tasked with projects including the design and construction of the [Salford Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salford_Central_railway_station "Salford Central railway station") bridges over New Bailey Road, replacing an older version.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52  In late 1843, Jacomb-Hood was employed by the M&BR again as an assistant to Baker, to work on the section of the railway between [Macclesfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macclesfield_railway_station "Macclesfield railway station") and [Cheadle Hulme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheadle_Hulme_railway_station "Cheadle Hulme railway station") (now part of the [Stafford–Manchester line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stafford%E2%80%93Manchester_line "Stafford–Manchester line")).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52  He began working on the line on 25 December 1843, and carried on through the first few months of 1844.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52

After he finished his work for the M&BR, he was then tasked with managing the parliamentary work of the [Manchester, South Junction and Altrincham Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester,_South_Junction_and_Altrincham_Railway "Manchester, South Junction and Altrincham Railway"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52  before being promoted to Resident Engineer of the railway from 1 September 1844.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 52–53  It is now known as the [Altrincham Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altrincham_Line "Altrincham Line"), which forms part of [Manchester Metrolink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Metrolink "Manchester Metrolink").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-23) He kept this role for two years until 1846.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) During his time as Resident Engineer he also worked with Baker on the [Shropshire Union Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire_Union_Canal "Shropshire Union Canal") and the Wilmslow & Knutsford Railway. However, he then turned down offers to work on the [Leeds Northern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_Northern_Railway "Leeds Northern Railway") and to start a partnership with Baker, instead deciding to apply for the new role as Resident Engineer on the [London, Brighton and South Coast Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London,_Brighton_and_South_Coast_Railway "London, Brighton and South Coast Railway").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53

### 1846–1850: Early LB&SCR work

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Jacomb-Hood&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1846–1850: Early LB&SCR work")\]

On 27 July 1846, the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway formed as an amalgamation of companies including the [London and Brighton Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_Brighton_Railway "London and Brighton Railway") and the [London and Croydon Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_Croydon_Railway "London and Croydon Railway").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-science-museum-group-24) Earlier that year on 6 May, Jacomb-Hood had attended a meeting of the provisional board as a candidate for the company's Resident Engineer. The sixty-two applicants were reduced to a shortlist of three,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  from which Jacomb-Hood was chosen and appointed from the company's creation.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-science-museum-group-24)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  He had a starting salary of £500,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  equivalent to £61,000 in 2023,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21) for which he was responsible for the construction, maintenance, and planning of the lines, stations, and goods depots.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53

[![Image 5: A black and white photo of a medium-sized brick building as taken from across the street. A canopy extends from the first floor with a white sign reading "STEYNING STATION"](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Steyning_railway_station_1861.jpg/250px-Steyning_railway_station_1861.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Steyning_railway_station_1861.jpg)

A photograph of [Steyning railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steyning_railway_station "Steyning railway station") on the [Steyning Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steyning_Line "Steyning Line"), taken on opening day in 1861.

In his first years at the company, his work mainly focussed on the completion of stations, managing contracts,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) and the railway's new stations at [London Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge_station "London Bridge station") and [Bricklayers Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bricklayers_Arms_railway_station "Bricklayers Arms railway station").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  He also designed and oversaw the construction of many branch lines, such as the [Cuckoo Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuckoo_Line "Cuckoo Line"), the [Seaford branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaford_branch_line "Seaford branch line"), and the [Steyning Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steyning_Line "Steyning Line").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  This was combined with the slow expansion of the [Brighton Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_Main_Line "Brighton Main Line") down to—and then along—the [South Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_of_England "South Coast of England").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  Jacomb-Hood was tasked with further expansion works during 1847, including the completion of the [Epsom Downs Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epsom_Downs_Branch "Epsom Downs Branch") in order to serve the upcoming [Epsom Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epsom_Derby "Epsom Derby"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  which took place that year on 19 May.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-25)

On 2 March 1847, Jacob-Hood was elected a Member of the [Institution of Civil Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institution_of_Civil_Engineers "Institution of Civil Engineers") (MICE).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) From May of the same year, Jacomb-Hood took in his brother George Jacomb-Hood as a pupil; the pair lived together in rented accommodation in [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton "Brighton").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  His work, however, did not always involve construction; for example, he was also tasked with converting the [Atmospheric Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_railway#London_and_Croydon_Railway "Atmospheric railway")—which had originally been built by the [London and Croydon Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_Croydon_Railway "London and Croydon Railway")[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-brennan-2020-26)—to steam running rather than by the use of pressure.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  The conversion finished on 4 May.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-brennan-2020-26) The rate of construction led to his salary (excluding bonuses) being increased to £750—equivalent to £92,000 in 2023[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21)—from 1 July 1847.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53

The economic success of Jacomb-Hood and the LB&SCR did not last long; by October 1847, Jacomb-Hood was set to be fired—along with the entire of his staff—due to the railway company being unable to find the money to complete more construction work. He gave his [resignation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resignation "Resignation") letter to the company on 3 January 1848, but it was overturned by a meeting of the board on 14 February as part of a wider investigation into the conduct and finances of the company. On 18 March, [Leo Schuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Schuster "Leo Schuster")—a board member—confirmed to Jacomb-Hood that he would be reappointed at the same salary, and his work was to be gradually resumed.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53

On 10 January 1849, Jacomb-Hood was appointed as the engineer to the [Portsmouth line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_line "Portsmouth line"), which was a joint project between the LB&SCR and the [London and South Western Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_South_Western_Railway "London and South Western Railway") (LSWR). The same year he also began giving out the contracts for London Bridge station, which first opened on 2 August 1850. Earlier that year, on 2 April, Jacomb-Hood had presented his paper titled _Description of a Vertical Lift Bridge erected over the Grand Surrey Canal[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-28)_ to the Institution of Civil Engineers; the paper details how he engineered the LB&SCR's [swing bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_bridge "Swing bridge") over the [Grand Surrey Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Surrey_Canal "Grand Surrey Canal") in London. The project, which ran between October 1848 and June 1849, had a total cost of £1300, which is equivalent to £165,000 in 2023.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21)[\[‡ 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-ice-bridge-27) The paper later won him a Council Premium of Books,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) which he was awarded by the Institution of Civil Engineers on 7 November 1850.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 54

### 1850–1860: Expansion of the LB&SCR

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Jacomb-Hood&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1850–1860: Expansion of the LB&SCR")\]

In the 1850s, the LB&SCR saw significant expansion and financial success.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) Due to the financial success of the railway, Jacomb-Hood's pay continued to increase and from 1852 he received an annual bonus proportionate to the [dividends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dividend "Dividend") of the company, and began investing. On 24 May 1852, Jacomb-Hood attended the first meeting of the Crystal Palace Board, the company responsible for the site in [Sydenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydenham,_London "Sydenham, London"), London onto which the [The Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") would be relocated. The board decided that a railway should be incorporated into the site;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 54  Jacomb-Hood was made responsible for the construction of this branch by the LB&SCR.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 54  The same year, he also began the enlargement of [London Bridge station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge_station "London Bridge station") and the construction of [Lewes railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewes_railway_station "Lewes railway station"), and the company moved into the new offices at the expanded London Bridge on 27 March 1854.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 54–55  He was also tasked by the LB&SCR with the construction of branch lines such as the [Arun Valley line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arun_Valley_line "Arun Valley line") and the [Oxted line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxted_line "Oxted line").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)

In February 1854, Jacomb-Hood hired [Guilford Lindsey Molesworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guilford_Lindsey_Molesworth "Guilford Lindsey Molesworth") as his assistant;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 55  Molesworth would later serve as the 41st President of the Institution of Civil Engineers from November 1904 to November 1905.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-Civ2-29) On 10 June 1850, Jacomb-Hood attended the opening of The Crystal Palace on its new site with his wife, having been responsible for the construction of the railway line serving it and later becoming a director on the board.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 54  By 1855, Jacomb-Hood's salary had reached £1059,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 55  equivalent to £125,000 in 2023.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21) In July of the same year, he also negotiated working privately on a new railway between Lewes and Uckfield (now part of the [Wealden Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wealden_Line "Wealden Line")); he would start this work on 7 August 1858 and would open on 11 October of the same year.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 56  The financial success of the LB&SCR—and that of Jacomb-Hood—continued through to the end of the 1850s; he was promised a salary of £1,200 from 1860, equivalent to £142,000 in 2023.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21) He also hired his younger brother John to work alongside him, tasking him with work in [Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth "Portsmouth") and [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne") before finding him a job in [Bombay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"), India (now Mumbai) in October 1858.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 56

> Many difficulties arise from the practice of employing architects to design and execute the station works. If, therefore, the Engineer desires to do full credit to his employers, and to himself, he should in all cases design the station works, either engaging assistants, or working conjointly with an architect, to furnish the necessary amount of architectural decoration, a talent for which is not always combined with constructive ability, or the faculty of judicious arrangement.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-collaborators-30)[\[‡ 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-paper-31)

Robert Jacomb-Hood, _The Arrangement and Construction of Railway Stations_ (1858)

On 27 April 1858, Jacomb-Hood submitted a paper to the Institution of Civil Engineers titled _The Arrangement and Construction of Railway Stations_.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-collaborators-30)[\[‡ 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-paper-31) In this paper, Jacomb-Hood argued that despite the average British railway engineer having little architectural training, the design of stations should nonetheless be their professional responsibility. He proposed the concept of 'judicious arrangement'; that is, that the functionality and logistics of a station was more important to its design than architectural grandeur. His assertion—based on this idea—that railway engineers should design their own stations, was highly innovative and unusual for the time.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-collaborators-30) On 14 December 1858, he was awarded a [Telford Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telford_Medal "Telford Medal") by the Institution of Civil Engineering for his work on the paper.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-journal-society-arts-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 56

A road curves around to serve the front of the building and there is a bus on the road and people on the pavement.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/London_Victoria_station_-14Oct2008.jpg/250px-London_Victoria_station_-14Oct2008.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:London_Victoria_station_-14Oct2008.jpg)

The façade of the LB&SCR half of [London Victoria railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station "London Victoria station"); the building was designed by Jacomb-Hood.

One of Jacomb-Hood's most prominent projects was the construction of [London Victoria railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station "London Victoria station"), which was to be the shared London terminus of the LB&SCR and the [London, Chatham and Dover Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London,_Chatham_and_Dover_Railway "London, Chatham and Dover Railway") (LC&DR). The station was built from two seemingly-unconnected buildings and financed equally by both railway companies.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-32) Jacomb-Hood was responsible for the design of the LB&SCR's half of the station; by applying his principle of judicious arrangement to the roof—built with a single truss design—the cost of the roof was reduced to £17 per 100 square feet (9.3 m2)—£2,000 in 2023[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21)—at a cost only two-thirds as expensive as the LC&DR's roof on the other side.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-swailes-2005-33) The station opened to passengers on 1 October 1860;[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-34) the roof does not survive today.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-swailes-2005-33)

### 1860–1869: Full-time private practice

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Jacomb-Hood&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1860–1869: Full-time private practice")\]

Alan A Jackson describes 1860 as a "milestone year" for Jacomb-Hood;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 57  on 29 September, Jacomb-Hood resigned as Resident Engineer due to the pressure of managing the parliamentary side of railway engineering.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 57 [\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-37) Instead, he chose to start practising privately as a civil engineer in [Westminster, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster"), but agreed to work on his ongoing projects until 31 December 1860 in return for a fee of £3,500[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 57  (equivalent to £415,000 in 2023).[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21) During his time in private practice, Jacomb-Hood worked on The [Arun Valley line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arun_Valley_line "Arun Valley line"), [South London line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_London_line "South London line"), and [Cranleigh line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cranleigh_line "Cranleigh line") among others.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) From 1860 to 1863, he worked with the British architect [Charles Driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Driver "Charles Driver") on projects including the [Dorking to Leatherhead line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_and_Mole_Valley_lines "Sutton and Mole Valley lines"), and [Portsmouth & Southsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_%26_Southsea_railway_station "Portsmouth & Southsea railway station") and [Tunbridge Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunbridge_Wells_railway_station "Tunbridge Wells railway station") railway stations.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-charles-driver-1) Having been employed by his brother in various ways (likely as a result of [nepotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism")), George Jacomb-Hood hosted a farewell party on 24 November 1863 before leaving the country to engineer the [Scinde Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scinde_Railway "Scinde Railway") in India, ending his pupilage.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58

In his early years of practising privately, Jacomb-Hood also collaborated with the engineer [George Parker Bidder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Parker_Bidder_/(engineer/) "George Parker Bidder (engineer)") on the construction of various projects.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 57  Despite the fact that Jacomb-Hood had left direct employment of the LB&SCR only a few years prior, the pair assumed all of the company's engineering works contractually from November 1863, splitting their profits evenly.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58  On 29 July 1864, the [Horsham, Leatherhead and Dorking Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsham,_Dorking_and_Leatherhead_Railway#Horsham,_Leatherhead_and_Dorking_Railway "Horsham, Dorking and Leatherhead Railway") was absorbed by the LB&SCR; the pair then finished the construction of the line together before it opened on 1 May 1867.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-38) The pair also worked on the [Portsmouth line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_line "Portsmouth line") between [Peckham Rye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peckham_Rye_railway_station "Peckham Rye railway station") and [Sutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_railway_station_/(London/) "Sutton railway station (London)") railway stations;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 57  the works on the section had finished by June 1867.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-39) They also worked on plans for the East London Railway (now partially the [East London line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London_line "East London line")) and the [Axminster and Lyme Regis Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axminster_and_Lyme_Regis_Railway "Axminster and Lyme Regis Railway"), among many others.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)

[![Image 7: A lithograph with only grey and cream colours. It features a man wearing a three-piece suit and bow tie leaning to his left; his left hand is on a chair and his right tucked into his blazer.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Robert_Jacomb-Hood.webp/250px-Robert_Jacomb-Hood.webp.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Jacomb-Hood.webp)

1865 [lithograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithograph "Lithograph") of Jacomb-Hood

In 1865, a portrait of Jacomb-Hood was made by the [lithographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") George B. Black; it is part of the [National Portrait Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Portrait_Gallery,_London "National Portrait Gallery, London")'s collection.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-40) On 3 July of the same year, Jacomb-Hood entered into a partnership with his cousin and former student William Jacomb;[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58  the pair practised in [Little George Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_George_Street "Little George Street") in the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster"), and branded their partnership as 'Jacomb and Hood'.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-london-gazette-1869-41) The agreement between them was that Jacomb would provide one third of the necessary capital in return for one third of the profits.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58  Together, they worked on projects across the United Kingdom, for example the Chichester and Midhurst Railway, which formed part of the [Midhurst Railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midhurst_Railways "Midhurst Railways"), and the [Bexleyheath line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bexleyheath_line "Bexleyheath line").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)

In December 1865, Jacomb-Hood travelled to Edinburgh with the intention of entering the competition to design [Edinburgh Waverley railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Waverley_railway_station "Edinburgh Waverley railway station").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58  However, the station redesign was instead carried out by James Bell, the Chief Engineer of the [North British Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_British_Railway "North British Railway"), based on a design for an extension he submitted in 1869. Due to the station remaining open during construction, these changes were not fully implemented until the 1870s.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-42)

On 28 April 1866, a bridge being built in [Sutton, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton,_London "Sutton, London") as part of Jacomb-Hood's work collapsed, killing six men. On 29 May of the same year, the LB&SCR stopped all its work due to the railway company being in financial difficulties, and Jacomb-Hood was instructed to withdraw or suspend all of the company's parliamentary proposals. However, he was still able to continue his work with the [South Eastern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Eastern_Railway_/(England/) "South Eastern Railway (England)") and the [London, Chatham and Dover Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London,_Chatham_and_Dover_Railway "London, Chatham and Dover Railway"), as well as assisting negotiations between the [Great Northern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_Railway_/(Great_Britain/) "Great Northern Railway (Great Britain)") and the [Edgware, Highgate and London Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgware,_Highgate_and_London_Railway "Edgware, Highgate and London Railway").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58  The financial situation of the LB&SCR had not improved by 1867, and the company descended into chaos with the appointment of an entirely new board of directors; this significantly jeopardised the company's abilities to pass legislation and continue constructing lines.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 59

In the late 1860s Jacomb-Hood also engaged in civil engineering works not directly related to the railways;[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) in 1867, he helped to complete the [ironwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironwork "Ironwork") on the roof of the [National Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery "National Gallery") building in London alongside his partner William Jacomb.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 59  The pair were then tasked by the [War Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Office "War Office") (now the [Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_/(United_Kingdom/) "Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)")[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-NationalArchives-C259-43)) in 1868 to plan repairs to the Portcreek Viaduct near [Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth "Portsmouth"), Hampshire; the works were then carried out during the following year.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 59–60  In December 1868, Jacomb-Hood also helped with the inspection of the harbour at [St Just in Penwith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Just_in_Penwith "St Just in Penwith"), Cornwall.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 59

In May 1869, Jacomb-Hood was given the title of Consulting Engineer at the LB&SCR in order for him to assist his successor, [Frederick Banister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Banister "Frederick Banister"), in his work; Jacomb-Hood then worked on once again reorganising the engineering department at the railway. In December 1869, William Jacomb was hired as the Resident Engineer of the [London and South Western Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_South_Western_Railway "London and South Western Railway"), because of which their partnership was dissolved on 31 December 1869 by mutual consent;[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-london-gazette-1869-41)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 60  he would hold this position from the start of 1870 until 1887.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-44) Combined with the death of his wife the same year (see [§ Personal life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#Personal_life)), this motivated Jacomb-Hood to end full time practice and enter semi-retirement, moving to a smaller office in Westminster.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 60

### 1869–1883: Semi-retirement

To make up for the subsequent loss of income, he accepted an invite to become a director of the [Crystal Palace Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") on 30 December 1869;[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 60  of its eight original board members, two were also board members of the LB&SCR.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-crystal-palace-45)[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-46) He also took an active part in his role at the Crystal Palace Company; in May 1870 he travelled to continental Europe in advance of the creation of the Crystal Palace Aquarium,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 60  which he would become heavily involved in the construction and management thereof.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) The project, which was led by the aquarist [William Alford Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Alford_Lloyd "William Alford Lloyd"),[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-crystal-palace-park-trust-47) involved building the first stand-alone [aquarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarium "Aquarium") outside of a zoo and by far the largest aquarium in the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles "British Isles") when it opened in 1871.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-48) However, it did not see financial success.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-crystal-palace-park-trust-47)

On 1 November 1870, Jacomb-Hood joined the board of the Anglo-Maltese Hydraulic Dock Company.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 60  Based in [Victoria Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Street,_London "Victoria Street, London"), London, they were constructing a dock in [Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malta "Malta") which used a hydraulic system to lift boats out of the water and into a [dry dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dry_dock "Dry dock"). The dock was finished in 1873 at a cost of £143,000,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-49) which is equivalent to £16,005,000 in 2023,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21) and Jacomb-Hood was sent to Malta to assist in the company's affairs in July 1872.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 60  He left the board in May 1877.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61
