The Chairman of the LB&SCR, [Samuel Laing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Laing_/(science_writer/) "Samuel Laing (science writer)"), commissioned Jacomb-Hood to travel to [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") and negotiate the purchase of the [Central Northern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Northern_Railway "Central Northern Railway") between [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba,_Argentina "Córdoba, Argentina") and [Tucumán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Miguel_de_Tucum%C3%A1n "San Miguel de Tucumán").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-museo-ferroviario-2015-51) Jacomb-Hood incorporated the visit into a wider holiday of his between January and May 1872, which included visits to [southeast Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Europe "Southeast Europe"), [West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa"), and the Atlantic coast of [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America") (see image for full route). He arrived back in the United Kingdom at [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton "Southampton") on 13 June. Upon his return, he gave up his last Westminster office, which closed on 8 July 1872.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  The railway was eventually bought by the British-owned [Córdoba Central Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba_Central_Railway "Córdoba Central Railway") in 1887.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-museo-ferroviario-2015-51)

[![Image 10: A bordered map on cream paper captioned "MAP OF THE / QUEEN & CRESCENT / ROUTE." On the map is a dense network of railway lines with a y-shaped boldened line running from the bottom-left to top right](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/1891_Poor%27s_Queen_and_Crescent_Route.jpg/250px-1891_Poor%27s_Queen_and_Crescent_Route.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1891_Poor%27s_Queen_and_Crescent_Route.jpg)

An 1891 map of the Alabama and Great Southern Railway Company; Jacomb-Hood was instrumental in its creation.

In 1877, he was commissioned by [Emile Erlanger & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emile_Erlanger_%26_Co. "Emile Erlanger & Co.") to assist in their decision whether or not to purchase the Alabama and Chattanooga Railway. He travelled to the United States with [Sir Philip Rose, 1st Baronet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Philip_Rose,_1st_Baronet "Sir Philip Rose, 1st Baronet") in order to inspect the line and write a report on it.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61 It was as a result of this report that the [Alabama Great Southern Railway Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_Great_Southern_Railway_Company "Alabama Great Southern Railway Company") was formed in 1877,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) and he served as a director of the company from September 1877 until 1886, helping in its setup alongside Charles Schiff.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  In 1879, he resigned as a board member of the Crystal Palace Company; the same year, he was commissioned for a second time by Emile Erlanger & Co., this time to assist with the company's undertakings in the [West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies") and the United States.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)

In 1876, the Thames Haven Petroleum Storage Company had begun building warehouses to store barrels of petroleum oil from the [Thameshaven port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thameshaven "Thameshaven"). It began operating in 1880,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-cracknell-1952-52) with Jacomb-Hood having been a director since November 1877;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  it maintained a monopoly on the import of petroleum into London until 1900.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-cracknell-1952-52) Charles Schiff had also convinced Jacomb-Hood to join the board of the New Gas Company in September 1878.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61

In October 1879, he collaborated once again with the same people who had commissioned the [Wealden Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wealden_Line "Wealden Line") between Lewes and Uckfield; this time, he was asked to help plan a restart of the never-completed [Ouse Valley Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouse_Valley_Railway "Ouse Valley Railway").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  The scheme never came to light and no work has been undertaken on the line since February 1869, when the LB&SCR made an agreement with the South Eastern Railway that rendered the line useless.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-53) In November 1879, there were mass resignations among the board of directors at the Crystal Palace Company, including the Chairman, Deputy Chairman, and Jacomb-Hood;[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-54)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-55)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  the following March he also left the board of the Thames Haven Petroleum Storage Co. In May 1880, he joined the board of the [Sydney and Louisburg Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_and_Louisburg_Railway "Sydney and Louisburg Railway");[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  situated in [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia"), Canada, the company's main role was to carry coal mined by the [Dominion Coal Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_Coal_Company "Dominion Coal Company"), but also carried passengers. The only extant remains of the railway are the station building in [Louisbourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisbourg "Louisbourg").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-56)

In May 1881, Jacomb-Hood submitted an entry to the design competition for [Liverpool Exchange railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Exchange_railway_station "Liverpool Exchange railway station"), something he had been working on since December of the previous year.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  On 3 August 1881, it was announced that John West had won the competition out of forty-three entrants, with the first part of the new station opening on 23 February 1888.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-57) He also served as a director of the [Assam Railways and Trading Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam_Railways_and_Trading_Company "Assam Railways and Trading Company") between August 1881 and February 1882,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  a British company that later became part of the Indian [Dibru–Sadiya Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dibru%E2%80%93Sadiya_Railway "Dibru–Sadiya Railway"). It was commissioned to build a line in modern-day [Assam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam "Assam") on 16 July 1883, which eventually closed on 12 December 2011.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-58)

### 1883–1900: Later work and death

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robert_Jacomb-Hood&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 1883–1900: Later work and death")\]

[![Image 11: A black and white photograph of a locomotive and its coal-wagon facing rightwards at a station platform. On the wheel casing reads "JACOMB HOOD".](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/LB%26SCR_B1_192_%28Jacomb-Hood%29.jpg/250px-LB%26SCR_B1_192_%28Jacomb-Hood%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LB%26SCR_B1_192_/(Jacomb-Hood/).jpg)

[LB&SCR B1 class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LB%26SCR_B1_class "LB&SCR B1 class") locomotive number 192, named in honour of Jacomb-Hood

On 7 March 1883, Jacomb-Hood was invited to join the LB&SCR's [board of directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors") as a replacement for the retiring [Sir Arthur Otway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Otway "Arthur Otway");[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 62  in the seventeen years between his appointment to the board and his death, he spent most of his time working on the LB&SCR's business.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) His early work as a director involved the restructuring of the engineering department at the railway and assisting on individual projects such as [Newhaven Harbour railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newhaven_Harbour_railway_station "Newhaven Harbour railway station").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 63

William Jacomb—the cousin of former partner of Jacomb-Hood—died suddenly on 26 May 1887; Jacomb-Hood was present at his funeral on 31 May the same year, which took place at [Wimbledon Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wimbledon_Cemetery "Wimbledon Cemetery").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 62  He gave up the seats he held on the boards of the Alabama Great Southern Railway Company and the Sydney and Louisburg Railway in 1886, ending his involvement in engineering in [the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas "Americas") that he had held since 1872.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61–62  Beginning in 1887, Jacomb-Hood also started attending the International Railway Congress; he was present at [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") in September 1887, [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") in September 1889, [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton "Brighton") in October 1891 (of particular significance as the southern terminus of the LB&SCR), and Paris in June 1893.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 62–63

[![Image 12: A colour painting of a mostly bald man leaning against a desk. He is holding a cane in his left hand and has his right hand on his hip. He is wearing a long coat and red jumper and looks stern and directly forward.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/George_Percy_Jacomb-Hood_%281857-1929%29_-_Portrait_of_an_Elderly_Gentleman_-_1977-5823_-_National_Railway_Museum.jpg/250px-George_Percy_Jacomb-Hood_%281857-1929%29_-_Portrait_of_an_Elderly_Gentleman_-_1977-5823_-_National_Railway_Museum.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Percy_Jacomb-Hood_/(1857-1929/)_-_Portrait_of_an_Elderly_Gentleman_-_1977-5823_-_National_Railway_Museum.jpg)

_Portrait of an Elderly Gentleman_ is believed to depict Robert Jacomb-Hood and was painted by his son George.

The LB&SCR dedicated one of their [B1 class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LB%26SCR_B1_class "LB&SCR B1 class") locomotives (known as "[Gladstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ewart_Gladstone "William Ewart Gladstone")") to Jacomb-Hood; number 192, named "Jacomb-Hood",[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-searle-2018-59)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-60) was an [0-4-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/0-4-2 "0-4-2") locomotive that entered service in November 1888. The name was removed c. 1906 and the locomotive left service in December 1927.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-searle-2018-59) The final year of his life in which he kept known diaries was 1894, by which point he was barely working and instead spent most of his time on holidays around the UK and Europe;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 63  he had only first visited mainland Europe on 29 May 1849, showing the extent of his financial success.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 53  He was present at the opening of the [Tower Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Bridge "Tower Bridge") in London on 9 July 1894, the last recorded association of his with a civil engineering project during his lifetime.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 63

The c. 1895 painting _Portrait of an Elderly Gentleman_ by George Percy Jacomb-Hood is believed to be a depiction of Robert Jacomb-Hood, his father. It is currently held in the archives of the [National Railway Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Railway_Museum "National Railway Museum"),[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-national-railway-museum-61) having been "obtained as a result of a direct claim of redundant material from the nationalised railway in 1977".[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-62) Little is known about the last six years of Jacomb-Hood's life beyond his [obituary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obituary "Obituary").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 63

Jacomb-Hood died suddenly in [Tunbridge Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tunbridge_Wells "Royal Tunbridge Wells") on 10 May 1900, aged 78. At the time, he was still working for the LB&SCR, and was also one of the longest serving members of the Institution of Civil Engineers, having been elected over 53 years before his death.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20) His grave is inscribed with [2 Timothy 4:7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_Timothy_4 "2 Timothy 4") as translated in the [King James Version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_Version "King James Version"): "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith".[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-63)[\[‡ 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-64) His obituary—published by the Institution of Civil Engineers—praised his dedication to the LB&SCR, saying that "he spared no pains to place at their service that keen intellect, fine memory and tactful discrimination for which he will be long remembered".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-obituary-20)

[![Image 13: A profile view of a young man with his head turned to face the viewer. He is wearing a blazer and bow tie and has short cropped hair and a moustache. It is a colour oil painting.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/George_Percy_Jacomb-Hood_-_Self_Portrait_NPG_6083.jpg/250px-George_Percy_Jacomb-Hood_-_Self_Portrait_NPG_6083.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Percy_Jacomb-Hood_-_Self_Portrait_NPG_6083.jpg)

A [self-portrait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-portrait "Self-portrait") of Jacomb-Hood's son George

On 25 November 1851,[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-65) Jacomb-Hood married Jane Stothard Littlewood. She was the daughter of George Littlewood, who was a local printer.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-ellisrees-2021-66) The pair had met earlier the same year, because she was the governess of his cousin's children.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 54 According to their marriage certificate, they were married at [St George's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George%27s,_Bloomsbury "St George's, Bloomsbury") in the [parish of Bloomsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomsbury "Bloomsbury") in [Middlesex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex "Middlesex") (now [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London")). He is described as a civil engineer and his father a "[gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentleman "Gentleman")"; neither had been previously married.[\[‡ 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-67)

Jacomb-Hood had nine children with his first wife, of whom two died in infancy; their first child Katie (who later took the surname Dale by marriage) was born on 27 April 1853.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 54  Their fourth child, [George Percy Jacomb-Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Percy_Jacomb-Hood "George Percy Jacomb-Hood"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-sellingantiques-13) was a successful painter and illustrator, and his work included depictions of his father.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-national-railway-museum-61)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-ellisrees-2021-66) His second son, [John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Wykeham_Jacomb-Hood&action=edit&redlink=1 "John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood (page does not exist)"), also became a civil engineer; his career included working as the Chief Engineer of the [London and South Western Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_South_Western_Railway "London and South Western Railway") and being elected to the Institution of Civil Engineers like his father.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-68)

On the death of his father on 9 July 1857,[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-69) Jacomb-Hood inherited the family seat at Bardon Hall in Bardon, Leicestershire. On 13 June 1864,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58  he sold the whole estate to William Percy Herrick of [Beaumanor Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaumanor_Hall "Beaumanor Hall") for £40,000,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-bulletin-of-the-loughborough-and-district-archaeological-society-1981-15)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-nuttall-1907-70) equivalent to £4,970,000 in 2023.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-inflation-UK-21) However, the conditions of his inheritance was that this money would be split equally among him and his siblings.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 58  He was the second and last member of his family to own the estate.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-walford-9)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-nuttall-1907-70)

On 27 November 1869, Jacomb-Hood's wife Jane, to whom he had been married for 17 years, died of "dropsical debility",[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 60  which refers to illness caused by an [oedema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edema "Edema"), a fluid-filled swelling beneath the skin.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-71) On 12 August 1870, Jacomb-Hood became engaged again to Elizabeth Thornton and on 21 February 1871 they married at [St George's, Hanover Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George%27s,_Hanover_Square "St George's, Hanover Square"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 60  in the [eponymous parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George_Hanover_Square "St George Hanover Square") in Middlesex (now London). His [marriage certificate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_certificate "Marriage certificate") once again listed him as a civil engineer; however, his now-dead father was listed as an "[esquire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquire "Esquire")" rather than simply a "[gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentleman "Gentleman")". Owing to the death of his former wife, he is described as a "[widower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widow "Widow")"; his wife was listed as a [spinster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinster "Spinster"), meaning that she had not been married previously.[\[‡ 9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-72) Elizabeth died suddenly in 1875 from cancer;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61  according to the inscription on her grave, she died on 10 January aged 46.[\[‡ 10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-73) He did not marry again, remaining a widower for the last twenty-five years of his life.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-jackson-1996-7): 61

Victoria is two stations in one, telling the story of intense rivalry between railway companies in the 19th century.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Located in the heart of London’s west end and offering speedy connections to seaside resorts, sea ports and Gatwick airport, Victoria Station has always been associated with train travel for pleasure.

![Image 1: historical drawing of Victoria station main building and hotel annexe](https://www.networkrail.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/history-of-london-vitoria-station.png)

### Competition for London’s West End

Competing for a line into the West End of London, the London Brighton & South Coast Railway (LBCSR) and the London Chatham & Dover Railway (LCDR) decided to pool their resources and back the Victoria Station & Pimlico Railway. This company had been authorised to build an extension of the line from the West End & Crystal Palace Railway’s ‘West End’ terminus (which was in fact across the river at Battersea), over the River Thames along with a new station at Victoria Street, just a few hundred yards from Buckingham Palace which was truly in the west end of the capital.

Access to Victoria Station was to be reached by the newly constructed Grosvenor Bridge, the first railway bridge to cross the Thames in London and designed for the Victoria Station & Pimlico Railway by John Fowler. Fourteen acres of land had been purchased for the new terminus.

The LBCSR’s side of the station, designed by their engineer Robert Jacomb Hood, was finished first and opened on 1 October 1860. The LCDR’s station on the east side of the site opened two years later on 25 August 1862 with a trainshed roof designed and constructed by their engineer Sir John Fowler.

### Two stations – two designs

To please the rich and influential residents of Pimlico and Belgravia, the railway companies had to enclose with a roof the tracks from the station back to Ecclestone Bridge, in order to protect them from the noise, soot and smoke of the steam engines. This meant that little money was left to create proper station buildings; both companies erected crude wooden huts which welcomed travellers on arrival, and these remained unchanged for the next forty years.

Both companies decided to upgrade their respective stations towards the end of the nineteenth century. The London Brighton & South Coast Railway moved first, buying the independent Grosvenor Hotel next to their part of the station in 1899 and extending it to form their new frontage. Designed by LBSCR’s chief engineer Sir Charles Morgan it was built in red brick and adorned with a large clock set in a scroll, giving it an elaborate Edwardian Baroque style to compliment the Grosvenor Hotel. The old trainshed roof was replaced to cover newly extended platforms which could receive longer trains. With an exclusive entrance in Buckingham Palace Road was also created for use by the royal family the new station opened in 1908.

### Two stations become one

Not to be outdone, the South Eastern & Chatham Railway (SECR), which the LDCR had joined in 1899, commissioned AW Blomfield to design a new station. The 1860s Fowler trainshed roof was retained; the main buildings were designed and constructed in a very different style to that of the LBSCR.

The SECR station was set slightly in front of its neighbour, and built in white Portland stone, to reinforce the separation between the two companies. This new station opened in 1909. This separation of the two stations was maintained until railway grouping in 1923 when both the LBSCR and the SECR became part of the Southern Railway. The Southern Railway set about integrating the two stations, opening up archways in the party walls that divided the two halves.

### International glamour

The glamour of holiday travel to Brighton and the Continent had been a feature of Victoria since the 1870s, but it was the early twentieth century saw the heyday of travel for pleasure from the station. In the 1930s services such as the Brighton Belle and the overnight ‘boat train’ services to France and Belgium were introduced.

Just before world war two, the Southern Railway briefly experimented with a new ‘flying boat’ service with a connection from Victoria to the new commercial airfield at Southampton. This connection with international travel was rejuvenated with the opening of Gatwick Airport in 1958 and the introduction of the first rail-air terminal at Victoria where passengers could check in to their flight prior to catching their flight at Gatwick. This developed into the Gatwick Express service, introduced in 1984.

### Victoria shopping

Victoria station has developed through the years, with recent additions being made to update passenger facilities. The 1980’s saw the removal of the ‘Brighton’ side roof to make way for Victoria Plaza – a multi-storey office and shop complex. In 1992 the station site was tidied and enlarged, with the two concourses becoming even more integrated through a series of matching shops built through the archway of the original dividing wall.

### Did you know?

Victoria Station was first referred to as the ‘Grosvenor Terminus’ as it was built on the site of old Grosvenor Canal basin. It was eventually named after nearby Victoria Street, rather than Queen Victoria.

AUTHOR: WILLIAM ELLIS-REES

PUBLISHED: 1 AUGUST 2021

![Image 1](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/hood.southwark-george-inn-yard.jpg)

The inner yard of the George Inn in Southwark. George Jacomb-Hood 1865. Southwark Heritage.

One of the more curious items in the heritage collections of Southwark Council is a drawing of the inner yard of the George Inn. The drawing was executed in May 1865 by George Percy Jacomb-Hood — more of whom later — and it is about ten inches in height and seven and three-quarters in width.

The view is of the entrance to a coach yard with two ostlers tending to a pair of horses. To the left of the entrance a cat sits on the flagstones with its back to us, watching the proceedings, while two birds fly across the picture from the right. The eye is drawn through the entrance to the yard itself, which is bathed in light.

![Image 2](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/hood.george-percy-jacomb-hood-scaled.jpg)

Self-portrait. George Percy Jacomb-Hood late 19th / early 20th century. National Portrait Gallery.

### Bertram Waldrom Matz

The George, which still stands, is London’s only surviving galleried coaching inn. On old maps one finds it lodged between White Hart Yard to the north and Talbot Yard to the south, both yards issuing into Borough High Street, which becomes Wellington Street before crossing the river over London Bridge. Time was when it was only one of many such establishments in [Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Southwark), all of which served the needs of travellers heading out of the capital along the great coaching routes.

In order to experience the George as it was in the days of Jacomb-Hood, one can do worse than leaf through a little monograph written by Bertram Waldrom Matz, which was published in 1918. Matz was a writer with a strong interest in [Charles Dickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dickens) and an editor of _[The Dickensian](https://www.dickensfellowship.org/index.php/read/the-dickensian)_ from 1905 to 1925, and he was fond of the George, which, along with Southwark generally, seemed to him to occupy an important space in the imaginative landscape of the great novelist.

![Image 3](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/hood.yard-george-inn-southwark.jpg)

The George Inn as it was in 1858. J. Sachs / Bertram Waldrom Matz _The George Inn, Southwark_ 1918.

### Mahogany this mahogany that

Indeed, when Matz describes the interior of the inn, he is quick to make illuminating references. The bar parlour, with its pewter pots and mahogany pulls, its polished casks and horse pistols, reminds him irresistibly of the equivalent room in the Six Jolly Fellowship-Porters in _Our Mutual Friend_. The coffee-room is

_such as the Pickwickians and their ancestors revelled in. The same old box compartments with their mahogany tables, seats and high-backed partitions; mahogany sideboards and occasional tables, where the joints are placed at meal-times; mahogany chairs with horse-hair seats to pull round the fire on winter days; casement windows, T-shaped gas jets, old prints; to say nothing of the red cord bell-rope still in working order by the side of the fireplace._

In a similar vein Matz lovingly describes the wood panelling and sawdust floor of the tap-room, the old-fashioned roasting-jack in the kitchen, the deal tables and plate warmer. In his mind’s eye he can see and hear the garrulous coachmen of the past — ‘the Tony Wellers of his day and before’ — smoking their long clay pipes and downing beer from tankards.

![Image 4](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/hood.potterson-six-jolly-fellowship-porters-scaled.jpg)

Miss Abbey Potterson and customer at the bar of the Six Jolly Fellowship-Porters. Marcus Stone / Charles Dickens _Our Mutual Friend_ 1865.

### Clubbable fellows

Matz also gives an amusing account of clubs that patronised the George. The Four O’Clockers, a group of local businessmen, dined there every day for almost thirty years, its wine-bill paid in part from the fines foisted on any member who turned up late for dinner, which was served, hardly surprisingly, at four o’clock.

The Old Chums, also businessmen, met for dinner on the first Saturday in each year, their ranks becoming depleted at the time of the Great War, when the tradition was just kept alive by a solitary member who on Saturday 5 January 1918 invited his wife to dine with him.

On one occasion members of The Most Secret Brotherhood of the Rolling Stones were ordered to present themselves at the George at _exactly_ thirty-one minutes past seven, knocking at the door three times and gaining admission to the meeting room by means of agreed signs.

![Image 5](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/hood.george-inn-coffee-room.jpg)

Coffee room at the George Inn in 1885. George Percy Jacomb-Hood / Bertram Waldrom Matz _The George Inn, Southwark_ 1918.

### Flitting ghosts

Other clubs and societies listed by Matz, who obviously had an ear for the music of peculiar names, are

_The Selborne Society, The Cult of London, Shakespearean Society, The London Co-operative Holiday Association, The Balham Antiquarian and Natural History Society and the Dickens Fellowship, the members of which, after visiting the many historic places of interest in the neighbourhood, bring their rambles to a fitting and appropriate end within the walls of the famous Inn._

On the subject of _The Pickwick Papers_ Matz has little patience with the suggestion that the White Hart Inn, where Sam Weller makes his first appearance in Chapter Ten, was closely modelled on the George. There is only one direct reference to the George in the novels — from Maggy in Chapter Twenty-Two of _Little Dorrit_ — and there was in any case a real White Hart in the nearby White Hart Yard! Even so it is not hard to ‘see’ Sam Weller among the other ghosts that flitted through the fine old coaching inn whenever aficionados of the novelist stopped there for a drink, or a meal, or a night’s stay.

![Image 6](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/hood.sam-weller-white-hart-inn.jpg)

Sam Weller ‘engaged in burnishing a pair of painted tops’ at the White Hart Inn. Hablot Knight Browne / Charles Dickens _The Pickwick Papers_ 1837.

### Jacomb-Hood

But to return to the subject with which we began. George Percy Jacomb-Hood, the creator of the drawing of the George, was born in 1857 in Redhill in Surrey. His father, Robert Jacomb-Hood, was a prominent railway engineer. His mother, Jane Stothard Littlewood, was the daughter of a printer, George Littlewood. He won a scholarship to the [Slade School of Fine Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_School_of_Fine_Art) to study under [Edward John Poynter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Poynter) and [Alphonse Legros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Legros), following which he travelled to Madrid, again with a scholarship, and to Paris, where he gained further experience under [Jean-Paul Laurens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Laurens) and [John Lavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lavery).

He was closely associated with the artistic mainstream, living and working at fashionable addresses in Kensington and Chelsea. He was a friend of [Whistler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Abbott_McNeill_Whistler) and a horse-riding companion of [Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Singer_Sargent), and he developed a fine reputation as a portrait painter. He was comfortable in high society — when he was in his fifties he married the daughter of the 8th Baron de Hochepied Larpent — and in 1911 he recorded the royal investiture ceremony in Delhi.

In fact Jacomb-Hood covered a number of royal visits to India as an artist-correspondent of _The Graphic_. Elsewhere, though, and in marked contrast to these high-profile commissions, he worked as a book illustrator, and some of his finest images are in that children’s staple, _[The Blue Fairy Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lang%27s_Fairy_Books)_. His enchanting Cinderella, to take just one example, captures wonderfully the aching unhappiness of the forsaken girl.

![Image 7](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/hood.fireplace-cinderella-scaled.jpg)

Cinderella sitting by the fireplace among the ashes. George Percy Jacomb-Hood / Andrew Lang _The Blue Fairy Book_ 1889.

### Documenting the North West

Jacomb-Hood exploited this sympathetic quality in a remarkable collaboration with [Leopold Hartley Grindon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Hartley_Grindon) in the 1890s. Grindon was known principally for his many books on botany, but his writing embraced such diverse subjects as the world of Manchester bankers and the nature of figurative language.

But the publication we are interested in here was a descriptive history of the county of Lancashire, which not only allowed Grindon to bring together his wide-ranging interests, but also gave Jacomb-Hood, who was one of several contributing illustrators, an opportunity to employ a social realist style that rivals the best work of [Luke Fildes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_Fildes) and [Hubert von Herkomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_von_Herkomer). His heroic images of working-class men and women achieve a wonderful synthesis of the physical splendour of his subjects with the grittiness and poverty of their surroundings.

![Image 8](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/hood.emigres-liverpool-scaled.jpg)

Emigrants at Liverpool. George Percy Jacomb-Hood / Leopold Hartley Grindon _Lancashire. Brief Historical and Descriptive Notes_ 1882.

### Old old old

By the time Jacomb-Hood died, which was in 1929, the George Inn had submitted to the deleterious effects of progress. In 1849 it was sold to the trustees of [Guy’s Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy%27s_Hospital), its neighbour. Later, in 1874, it was bought by the [Great Northern Railway Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_Railway_/(Great_Britain/)) for a sum in the region of eleven thousand pounds. A portion of the building was destroyed to make room for a receiving-house, where a hundred tons of goods were weighed every day.

However, the work of destruction was never completed, and the George lived on, albeit maimed, where other coaching inns disappeared without trace. Bertram Waldrom Matz, who dearly loved the inn and all it stood for, finds many apt phrases. ‘The last of its race.’ ‘An unspoiled survival’ — for all the efforts of the demolishers — ‘of old London.’ ‘The rendezvous of a continual flow of literary and antiquarian enthusiasts.’

![Image 9](https://london-overlooked.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/hood.george-inn-southwark-yard.jpg)

The George Inn as it was in 1889. Bertram Waldrom Matz _The George Inn, Southwark_ 1918.

But for his definitive comment on the unique charm of the Southwark hostelry Matz resorts to a literary reference. In Act One of _She Stoops to Conquer_ [Goldsmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Goldsmith) introduces Mr Hardcastle as a man who loves ‘everything that’s old’, namely ‘old friends, old times, old manners, old books, old wine’. According to Matz it is this attachment to the past, and to its faded glories, that explains the very special appeal of a building that still serves as a reminder of a bygone age.

1850 Jacomb Hood presented his paper entitled _Description of a Vertical Lift Bridge erected over the Grand Surrey Canal_ to the Institution of Civil Engineers [\[1\]](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-1)

* * *

**1900 Obituary [\[2\]](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Robert_Jacomb-Hood#cite_note-2)**

ROBERT JACOMB-HOOD, eldest son of the late Mr. Robert Jacomb, who assumed subsequently the name of Hood, of Bardon Park, Leicestershire, was born at Riseley, in Bedfordshire, on the 25th January, 1822, and received his preliminary education at Christ’s Hospital.

To meet the wishes of his father he was specially prepared, on leaving school, with a view to the Bar as a profession, and kept several terms at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1840 and 1841. He had, however, been thrown previously with young men who were engaged on railway construction in the Midlands, and by them he was imbued with a desire to become an engineer.

His father’s objections having been overcome, Robert Jacomb-Hood, in the year 1841, became an articled pupil of [Mr. George Watson Buck](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/George_Watson_Buck "George Watson Buck"), then Chief Engineer, in conjunction with [Robert Stephenson](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Robert_Stephenson "Robert Stephenson"), of the [Manchester and Birmingham Railway](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Manchester_and_Birmingham_Railway "Manchester and Birmingham Railway"). Under Mr. Buck, Mr. Jacomb-Hood became Assistant on the Holmes Chapel length of the line to [Mr. William Baker](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/William_Baker "William Baker"), afterwards Chief Engineer of the London and North Western Railway; and on the Crewe length to [Mr. W. H. Barlow](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/William_Henry_Barlow "William Henry Barlow"), Past-President.

When the line was opened to Crewe in 1843 Mr. Jacomb-Hood was engaged as Chief Assistant by Mr. Buck, who had then severed his connection with the Company to take private practice in Manchester. In that capacity he was employed among other works in the rebuilding of the New Bailey Bridge at Salford.

Subsequently he again became an Assistant to Mr. William Baker on the engineering staff of the Manchester and Birmingham line, having been appointed for the construction of the Macclesfield branch. Between 1844 and 1846 he acted as Resident Engineer on the Manchester, South Junction and Altrincham line.

In 1846 Mr. Jacomb-Hood was appointed Resident Engineer to take charge of the whole of the system of the [London, Brighton and South Coast Railway Company](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/London,_Brighton_and_South_Coast_Railway "London, Brighton and South Coast Railway"). This was the beginning of a connection which lasted in one form or another for fifty-four years. In the early days of his appointment as Engineer to the Brighton Company Mr. Jacomb-Hood was engaged chiefly in completing stations and works in progress, in arranging maintenance contracts, and on the construction of the new London Bridge Station, and of the Bricklayers Arms Goods Station. He also laid out and completed the Newhaven, Eastbourne and Hailsham, Epsom, Croydon and Wandsworth, Littlehampton and Steyning branches.

In 1880 Mr. Jacomb-Hood was awarded a Council Premium of Books by the Institution for his "Description of the Lift Bridge over the Grand Surrey Canal, on the line of the Thames Junction Branch of the London, Blighton and South Coast Railway,” and in 1858 he obtained a Telford Medal for a Paper entitled “The Arrangement and Construction of Railway Stations."

Between the years 1850-60 the Brighton Company were fully engaged in developing their property, and it fell to Mr. Jacomb- Hood within that period to lay out the Crystal Palace branch, the East Grinstead branch, the Midhurst branch, the [Lewes and Uckfield](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Lewes_and_Uckfield_Railway "Lewes and Uckfield Railway"), and Shoreham and Henfield lines - while at the same time he was engaged on the [Victoria Station](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Victoria_Railway_Station "Victoria Railway Station") project and the enlargement of [Brighton Station](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Brighton_Railway_Station "Brighton Railway Station"), as well as on other heavy works.

So severe became the pressure of Parliamentary work that, in September, 1860, Mr. Jacomb-Hood resigned the post of Resident Engineer to the Brighton Company, retaining their Parliamentary and new works, and took up private practice in Westminster.

The Mid-Sussex and South London lines were carried out by him at that time, as well as the Croydon and Balham, the Horsham and Guildford, and Horsham and Dorking lines, the Seaford Extension, the Brighton, Uckfield, and Tunbridge Wells, and the Bognor branches.

In 1863, in conjunction with [Mr. G. P. Bidder](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/George_Parker_Bidder "George Parker Bidder"), he was busy on the Peckham and Sutton and Leatherhead and Dorking lines, and on Newhaven Harbour Improvements, as well as on plans for the Hadlow line, East London Railways, Axminster and Lyme, Southend and Malden, Ouse Valley and Hastings, Kingsland and Finsbury lines, and tramways at Southsea.

Mr. Jacomb-Hood was joined by his cousin and former pupil, [William Jacomb](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/William_Jacomb "William Jacomb"), as partner in 1865, and together they deposited schemes for railways in many parts of the country, including the Surrey and Sussex, Hornsey and Kingsland, West Kent, Chichester and Midhurst, Peckham and Dartford, and Norwood and Crystal Palace High Level lines, and a branch line from Bridport to Lyme.

Works undertaken subsequently to the above date include the preparation of the details of the ironwork for the National Gallery and the re-building of Portcreek Viaduct.

In 1869 Mr. Jacomb-Hood became a Director of the [Crystal Palace Company](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Crystal_Palace_Co "Crystal Palace Co"), and in the following year he dissolved partnership with Mr. William Jacomb, on the latter’s appointment as Chief Engineer to the London and South Western Railway Company.

He took an active part in the construction and organization of the Crystal Palace Aquarium and in the affairs of the Company generally, until he resigned his seat at the Board in 1879. In 1870 he joined the Board of the Anglo-Maltese Hydraulic Dock Company, and was employed on several occasions in investigating the affairs of that company at Malta.

In 1872 he was commissioned by the late [Mr. Samuel Laing](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/S._Laing "S. Laing"), then Chairman of the [Brighton Railway Company](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/London,_Brighton_and_South_Coast_Railway "London, Brighton and South Coast Railway"), to proceed to South America to negotiate a contract for the [Cordova and Tucuman Railway](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Cordova_and_Tucuman_Railway "Cordova and Tucuman Railway"), and a few years later he was engaged on behalf of [Messrs. Erlanger and Co.](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/index.php?title=Erlanger_and_Co&action=edit&redlink=1 "Erlanger and Co (page does not exist)") to examine the property and report on a proposal to purchase the undertaking of the [Alabama and Chattanooga Railway](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Alabama_and_Chattanooga_Railway "Alabama and Chattanooga Railway") in the United States. The result of the last investigation was the formation in 1877 of the [Alabama Great Southern Railway Company](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Alabama_Great_Southern_Railway "Alabama Great Southern Railway"), of which Mr. Jacomb-Hood was a Director until 1886.

On a subsequent occasion, in 1879, he was again commissioned by Messrs. Erlanger to investigate the affairs of other undertakings in the West Indies and in the Southern States of America.

Subsequently to 1880 he acted as a Director of several undertakings, including the [Thames Haven Petroleum Storage Company](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/index.php?title=Thames_Haven_Petroleum_Storage_Co&action=edit&redlink=1 "Thames Haven Petroleum Storage Co (page does not exist)"), the [New Gas Company](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/index.php?title=New_Gas_Co&action=edit&redlink=1 "New Gas Co (page does not exist)"), the [Sydney and Louisburg Railway and Coal Company](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/index.php?title=Sydney_and_Louisburg_Railway_and_Coal_Co&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sydney and Louisburg Railway and Coal Co (page does not exist)"), and the [Assam Railways and Trading Company](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Assam_Railways_and_Trading_Co "Assam Railways and Trading Co"), in the business of all of which he displayed that honesty of purpose and practical ability which distinguished him throughout his career.

In March, 1883, on the retirement of [Sir Arthur Otway](https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/index.php?title=Arthur_Otway&action=edit&redlink=1 "Arthur Otway (page does not exist)"), Mr. Jacomb-Hood was invited to accept a seat on the board of the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway Company, and in this way he renewed the close connection with which his earlier years were associated. For the last seventeen years of his life he devoted almost all his energies to the business of the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway Company. His whole interests were centred in the Company’s affairs, and he spared no pains to place at their service that keen intellect, fine memory and tactful discrimination for which he will be long remembered.

In almost full vigour of health he died suddenly at Tunbridge Wells, on the 10th May, 1900, in the 79th year of his age, having been engaged on the day of his death in transacting business for the Brighton Company.

Mr. Jacomb-Hood was one of the oldest Members of the Institution, having been elected to that class on the 2nd March, 1847.

Lifting Bridge near New Cross station, carrying the LBSCR branch over the Grand Surrey Canal. 1849-50](https://rchsimagearchive.org.uk/cache/Canals-Inland-Waterways/River-Thames/London-Bridge-to-Tilbury-Ness/079904E-Deptford-Wharf-Branch_220_thumb.jpg?cached=1744729421) #### Deptford Wharf Branch Railway (DPW). Lifting Bridge near New Cross station, carrying the LBSCR branch over the Grand Surrey Canal. 1849-50 Grid Ref: TQ 3575 7796. The "vertical lift bridge" bridge (Map Ref TQ 35745 77965) consisted of a rectangular platform of timber, carrying on one side the railway line and, on the other, a roadway for carts, and resting, when down, upon piles driven into a bed of hard gravel. The platform was suspended at the four corners by wire ropes, which passed over pulleys fixed on four pairs of cast- iron standards (also supported on piles), and then attached to drums, each pair of which were keyed on to the same horizontal shaft, lying a few inches under the rail and road level. Upon the same shafts were also fixed six other drums of equal diameter, carrying, upon coils of wire rope, balance weights, intended to assist in raising the platform , and which moved up and down cast-iron cylinders, or wells prepared to receive them. Motion was given to one end of each shaft, by means of simple hand-gearing, consisting of a train of wheels and pinions, by which the power was multiplied twenty-six times. The outside width of the platform was 23 feet, equally divided between the railway and the road, and the length was 35 feet; but the clear waterway in the canal was only 21 feet on the square, the additional length arising from the direction of the line being slightly askew to the canal, and from the necessity of leaving a clear width of 54 feet for a towing-path on the north bank. The level of the rails upon the bridge, when down, was 4 feet 2½ inches above the highest water-line, and the platform was capable of being raised so as to give a clear headway of 9 feet 6 inches below the tension rods, which was the height required by the Act for the fixed bridge erected over the same canal, at the second crossing near Deptford. The weight of the entire platform, with all the fittings complete, was about 12 tons, when the timber was dry. The drawing is included in the paper describing the bridge, its design, and construction, by Robert Jacomb Hood, M.I.C.E., (from which the above information is extracted), and contained in the Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers for the 1849-50 Session (page 303). It is clear that the bridge underwent a number of structural changes during its life, including that, by the time the area was surveyed in 1868, the roadway section had gone and the bridge comprised just that for a single railway line. However, alongside but separate, was a second lifting bridge whose purpose is not certain but which appears to be a roadway crossing.
